But in the savage tirade against Chantilly printed in yesterday’s ‘Musée,’ the satirist, with some shameful references to the cobbler’s change of name when he took to the stage, cited a Latin verse we have frequently discussed. I refer to the line

Perdidit antiquum litera prima sonum.

“I had explained that this referred to Orion, once spelled Urion; and certain pointed details of that explanation assured me you could not have forgotten it. Plainly, then, you would connect the thought of Orion with that of Chantilly. The particular smile that crossed your lips showed me that you had indeed joined them. You were considering the poor cobbler’s sacrifice. Until then you had walked with a stoop, but at that moment I watched you straighten to your full height. I knew then that you were thinking of Chantilly’s small stature. Here I broke into your reflections by observing that, since Chantilly was in fact such a little fellow, he would be better suited to the Théâtre des Variétés.”

Soon afterward, while we were examining an evening number of the “Gazette des Tribunaux,” the following paragraphs caught our attention.

“Extraordinary Murders.—At about three this morning, residents of the Quartier St. Roch were awakened by a series of appalling screams, apparently coming from the fourth floor of a house in the Rue Morgue, occupied, as was known, solely by Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, Mademoiselle Camille L’Espanaye. After some delay spent trying unsuccessfully to gain entrance in the ordinary way, the gateway was forced with a crowbar. Eight or ten neighbors entered, together with two gendarmes. The screams had by then stopped; but as the group hurried up the first staircase, two or more harsh voices could be heard angrily disputing, seemingly in the upper part of the house. By the time they reached the second landing, these voices too had fallen silent, and complete stillness prevailed. The group separated and rushed from room to room. On reaching a large rear chamber on the fourth floor—whose door they forced open after finding it locked with the key inside—they encountered a scene that filled everyone present with equal horror and amazement.

“The room was in utter confusion, its furniture smashed and scattered in every direction. There was only one bedstead; the bedding had been taken from it and flung into the center of the floor. A razor smeared with blood lay upon a chair.”

Col. Grangerford was a gentleman, you understand. A gentleman clear through, and his family was the same. He came of good blood, as folks say, and that counts for as much in a man as in a horse, according to the Widow Douglas. Nobody ever disputed that she belonged to the very first aristocracy in our town; and pap said so too, though he had no more quality about him than a mudcat. Col. Grangerford was mighty tall and slender, with a sort of dark-pale skin and not a speck of red in it. Every morning his narrow face was shaved clean, and he had the thinnest lips and nostrils you ever saw, a high nose, thick eyebrows, and eyes as black as could be, set so far back they looked like they was peering at you out of caves. His forehead was high, and his straight black hair reached his shoulders. His hands was long and spare. Each day of his life he wore a fresh shirt and a whole suit of linen, head to foot, so white it fairly hurt to look at it; Sundays he put on a blue tailcoat with brass buttons. He carried a silver-headed mahogany cane. There wasn’t anything foolish about him, not a particle, and he never talked loud. He was as kind as a body could be—you could sense it, and that made you trust him. Now and then he smiled, and it was a pleasant thing to see. But when he drew himself up straight as a liberty pole and lightning started flashing from beneath those eyebrows, you felt like getting up a tree first and asking what was wrong later. He never needed to tell folks to behave; wherever he was, everybody had good manners. They liked having him there, too. Most times he was sunshine—I mean, he made you feel the weather was fine. If he changed to a bank of clouds, it got fearfully dark for half a minute, which was plenty; nothing would go amiss again for a week.

When he and the old lady came downstairs mornings, the whole family rose from their chairs and wished them good-day, and nobody sat again before they did. Then Tom and Bob went over to the sideboard with the decanter, mixed him a glass of bitters, and brought it to him. He held it till they had fixed their own drinks. Then they bowed and said, “Our duty to you, sir, and madam”; and the old people gave the smallest little bows and thanked them. All three drank, and Bob and Tom added a spoonful of water to the sugar and the drop of whisky or apple brandy left in their tumblers, and handed them to Buck and me, so we drank to the old people as well.

After they had shared their distress over the terrible consequences of this affair, which Elizabeth thought almost inevitable and Miss Bennet could not call entirely impossible, Elizabeth returned to the subject. “But tell me everything I haven’t heard yet. Give me more details. What did Colonel Forster say? Had they suspected nothing before the elopement? They must have seen the two of them together constantly.”

“Colonel Forster admitted he had often suspected some affection, particularly on Lydia’s side, but nothing that alarmed him. I feel so sorry for him. He was as considerate and kind as anyone could be. He was already planning to come here to express his concern before he had any idea they might not have gone to Scotland. When that fear first arose, he hurried his journey.”

“And was Denny certain Wickham wouldn’t marry her? Did he know they intended to run away? Had Colonel Forster spoken to Denny himself?”

“Yes, but when the colonel questioned him, Denny denied knowing anything about their plan and would not give his true opinion. He did not repeat his conviction that they would not marry, which makes me hope he may have been misunderstood before.”

“And until Colonel Forster arrived, I suppose none of you doubted that they really were married?”

“How could such an idea have occurred to us? I was a little uneasy, a little afraid for my sister’s happiness as his wife, because I knew he had not always behaved quite properly. My father and mother knew nothing of that; they thought only of how unwise the marriage must be. Kitty then admitted, with a very natural satisfaction at knowing more than the rest of us, that Lydia’s last letter had prepared her for such a step. Apparently she had known for many weeks that they were in love.”

“But not before they went to Brighton?”

“No, I don’t believe so.”

“And did Colonel Forster himself seem to think badly of Wickham? Does he know what he is really like?”

“I must admit he did not speak as favorably of Wickham as he used to. He considered him reckless and extravagant, and since this unhappy affair people have said he left Meryton heavily in debt. But I hope that is untrue.”

“Oh, Jane, if we had been less secretive, if we had told people what we knew about him, this could never have happened!”

“Perhaps that would have been better,” her sister replied.

“But revealing someone’s past faults without knowing how they felt now seemed unjustifiable.”
